# string

Immutable Unicode text.

## Overview

A `string` is a sequence of **symbols** (Unicode code points). The symbol is the element everywhere on the
type: `len()` counts symbols, `s[i]` yields a `rune`, `s[i:j]` slices at symbol boundaries, and every member
offset — `index()`, `slice()`, `splice()`, `insert()` — is symbol-based.

```go
"héllo".len()        // => 5 — symbols, not bytes
"héllo"[1]           // => 'é' — a rune
"héllo"[1:3]         // => "él"
"abc"[-1]            // => 'c' — negative indices count from the end
"кавун".len()        // => 5
```

Symbols are code points, **not** grapheme clusters. A flag emoji is two regional-indicator symbols; a
combining sequence is a base symbol plus combining marks. What a reader perceives as one character can be
several symbols:

```go
"🇺🇦".len()          // => 2 — two regional indicators
"e\u0301".len()     // => 2 — é written as e + U+0301 (combining acute)
```

**Storage and cost.** A `string` is stored as compact UTF-8 with a cached symbol count and an ASCII fast
path: indexing and slicing are O(1) on pure-ASCII strings and O(n) worst case on multibyte content. For heavy
positional work on non-ASCII text, convert to [`runes`](runes.md) first — `runes` is the O(1)-indexing,
materialized form of the same text.
Members whose answer depends on the ends of the text or on the argument alone — `first`/`last`, the anchored pair
and their `remove_` twins, the `trim` family, the pads, and `contains`/`count`/`index`/`index_last`/`replace` —
read the text in place and never decode the whole receiver; the members that visit or rebuild every symbol decode
it once per call.

**Immutability.** A `string` is immutable by construction. It is the only sequence type with no mutating
member at all: no `_in_place` twins, and no `slice_view`/`chunk_view` (on an immutable value sharing is
unobservable, so `slice` *is* the view). Element assignment raises:

```go
s := "abc"
s[0] = 'x'           // Error: not_assignable: type string does not support assignment
```

A `string` literal is a compile-time constant as well: its content is fixed in the source, so the compiler
stores it once in the bytecode's static pool and every evaluation loads that one shared value. For `string`
this is invisible — the type has no mutating member either way — but it is the same mechanism that makes
`b"..."` and `u"..."` immutable *constants* of otherwise mutable types, and the reason all three short forms
exist: text written down in a program is usually constant text. See [Constant literals and constructed
literals](../../language.md#constant-literals-and-constructed-literals); when you want a mutable buffer of the
same content, construct one — `runes("abc")` or `bytes("abc")`.

**`string` and `runes` are semantically interchangeable** — the same text, the same member surface, the same
operator behavior, and they compare equal on equal content (`"ab" == u"ab"` is `true`). The difference is
storage (UTF-8 vs. a symbol array) and mutability. Choose `string` by default; choose `runes` when you need
in-place mutation or guaranteed O(1) indexing.

Every transforming member returns a new `string`; partitioning members (`split`, `partition`, `split_lines`,
`chunk`) return an `array` of strings.

The edge members `first([d])`, `last([d])`, `min([d])` and `max([d])` answer a `rune`; an empty string has no edge
to give, so without the optional trailing default they raise `invalid_value`:

```go
"abc".first()        // => 'a'
"".first()           // Error: invalid_value: (first) empty sequence
"".first('?')        // => '?'
"banana".min()       // => 'a'
"banana".max()       // => 'n'
```

The parsing conversions (`int`, `float`, `decimal`, `bool`, `time`, `date`, `nanoseconds`) follow the uniform
failure policy: a valid result or a catchable raise, and with the optional trailing default, the default when the
text does not parse. A malformed `time`/`date` layout is the caller's error, not the data's, and raises even with a
default. The re-representations `runes()`, `bytes()` and `array()` are total — they cannot fail — so they take no
default.

## Literals

```go
s := "hello"
esc := "line1\nline2 \"quoted\" \u00a0"   // escape sequences
raw := r"C:\Users\Bob \d+"                 // raw string: backslashes literal
uni := u"кавун"                             // a runes literal — same text, runes type
```

The free `string(x)` constructor is the conversion — the free spelling of `x.string()`. The two-argument
`string(x, n)` is the count form: the conversion repeated `n` times, `string(x).repeat(n)`:

```go
string()             // => ""
string("ab", 2)      // => "abab" — the count form: string(x).repeat(n)
string('x', 3)       // => "xxx"
string(65, 2)        // => "6565" — the conversion first: string(65) is "65"
```

F-strings interpolate expressions and format specs into a `string`: `f"n={n:5d}"`. See
[f-strings](../../f_strings.md) and the [format mini-language](../../format_mini_language.md).

## Operators

| operator | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `+` | concatenation of text content |
| `-` | remove every occurrence of the run (leftmost, non-overlapping), read as symbols as `remove` reads it — the octets of an escape never match inside a symbol; acceptance equals `+`'s |
| `*` | exactly `repeat(n)`: the right operand is a **count**, not text. No reflected direction — `n * s` raises |
| `==` `!=` | content equality; `string` and `runes` with the same text are equal |
| `<` `<=` `>` `>=` | lexicographic by symbol |
| `x in s` | membership — runs `contains`' value readings |
| `s[i]` | the symbol at `i`, as a `rune` |
| `s[i:j]` | symbol-boundary slice, a `string` |

Both operands must carry **text content**. The **receiver (left operand) decides the result type**; a scalar
on the left takes the sequence's type:

```go
"ab" + "cd"          // => "abcd"
"ab" + u"cd"         // => "abcd" — string — the left operand decides
u"ab" + "cd"         // => u"abcd" — runes on the left
"ab" + bytes("cd")   // => "abcd" — the bytes decode; the decode never fails
b'a' + "bc"          // => "abc" — scalar left takes the sequence's type
'é' + "bc"           // => "ébc"
"abc" + b'\xff'      // Error: invalid_value: a byte is a symbol only in ASCII (0x00–0x7F)
"ab" + 1             // Error: invalid_binary_operator: operators never take int — arithmetic keeps its reading
"ab" + 1.5           // Error: invalid_binary_operator
"ab" + true          // Error: invalid_binary_operator
"ab" + ["cd"]        // => ["ab", "cd"] — string declines; the array prepends it as one element
"ab" - ["cd"]        // Error: invalid_binary_operator: string - array (there is no reflected form for removal)
```

`-` removes runs or single symbols, never set-difference:

```go
"banana" - "na"      // => "ba" — every occurrence, leftmost non-overlapping
"banana" - 'a'       // => "bnn"
"banana" - 97        // Error: invalid_binary_operator: operators never take int

"-" * 20             // => "--------------------" — the count form of repeat
"ab" * 2.0           // => "abab" — a whole-valued count converts; 1.5 raises
2 * "ab"             // Error: invalid_binary_operator: int * string   (no reflected direction)
```

`in` accepts exactly the values `contains` accepts and raises on anything else — a callable raises, because
an operator operand is always a value, never a predicate:

```go
'a' in "abc"                       // => true
"bc" in "abc"                      // => true
97 in "abc"                        // => true — 'a' — members read a valid int as the symbol
1.5 in "abc"                       // Error: invalid_argument_type
(func(c) { return true }) in "abc" // Error: invalid_value — the predicate spelling is contains(f)
```

Comparisons are lexicographic by symbol, not by length:

```go
"abc" < "abd"        // => true
"b" > "aaaa"         // => true
```

## Argument dispatch

Every member and operator on `string` reads its arguments the same way. An argument is accepted iff it is
**text content encoded into the receiver's representation**:

| argument | reading |
| --- | --- |
| `string` / `runes` | text, verbatim — a contiguous **run** |
| `bytes` | decoded as UTF-8; **total** — an octet that is not a symbol becomes its [escape](#undecodable-octets) |
| `rune` | itself — one symbol |
| `byte` | one symbol iff ASCII (`0x00`–`0x7F`); beyond raises |
| `int` (members only) | one symbol iff a valid code point; **operators never take `int`** |
| `bool` / `float` / `decimal` | raise — a number as text is ambiguous (`65` could be `"65"` or `'A'`) |
| `int` (`*` only) | a repeat **count** — `s * n` is exactly `s.repeat(n)`; there is no reflected `n * s` |
| `array` / `range` / `dict` / callables / `undefined` | raise — the text family is closed. One exception is not `string`'s doing: `"ab" + [1, 2]` → `["ab", 1, 2]`, because a left operand that declines hands `+` to the array, which prepends it as one element (see [array](array.md)) |

The match members (`contains`, `count`, `index`, `index_last`, `keep`, `remove`, `any`, `all`, `split`, …)
share one argument menu:

- **no argument** — the [blank set](#the-blank-set);
- **a function** — a predicate: it gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument
([callbacks](#callbacks));
- **`string`/`runes`/`bytes`** — a contiguous run;
- **`rune`/`byte`/valid `int`** — one element;
- **variadic** — a homogeneous set: all elements or all runs. Mixing the two classes raises, and a function
among several arguments raises.

```go
"abc".contains('x', 'b')                       // => true — element set
"abc".count(func(i, c) { return i > 0 })       // => 2 — accepts two, not one: gets (index, element)
"abcd".remove("ab", "abc")                     // => "d" — run set; at a tie the longest run wins
"banana".remove("na", 'b')                     // Error: invalid_argument_type: mixed element and run classes
"abc".remove("a", func(c) { return true })     // Error: invalid_argument_type: a function among several arguments
```

The one exception is the **add side** (`append`/`prepend`), where operands mix freely in order:
`x.append("ab", 'c')` ≡ `x + "ab" + 'c'`.

Run matching is leftmost and non-overlapping: `"aaa".count("aa")` is `1`.

## Undecodable octets

Text that is not valid UTF-8 is data too — a file off disk, a legacy export, a truncated frame. So **every
conversion among `byte`, `bytes`, `string` and `runes` is total and lossless**: nothing raises, nothing is
substituted, and the octets you started with are the octets you get back.

An octet no decoder can read as a symbol becomes its own reserved rune — **U+DC80–U+DCFF, one per octet
0x80–0xFF** — and encoding turns that rune straight back into the octet it came from.

```go
b = bytes([0x61, 0xFF, 0x62])   // 'a', a stray octet, 'b'
s = b.string()                  // no raise
s.len()                         // => 3 — the octet is one symbol
s[1].int()                      // => 56575 — U+DCFF, the escape for 0xFF
s.bytes() == b                  // => true
s.runes().bytes() == b          // => true — through runes and back, unchanged
```

Asking, and repairing:

```go
s := bytes([0x61, 0xFF, 0x62]).string()
s.is_valid()                    // => false — some symbol is an escape
"abc".is_valid()                // => true
s[1].is_valid()                 // => false — this one
s[1].byte()                     // => byte(255) — the escape converts back to its octet
s.replace(s[1], '?')            // => "a?b"
s.keep(c => c.is_valid())     // => "ab"
```

**Why this range, and why it cannot go wrong.** Only an octet ≥ 0x80 can ever be undecodable — an ASCII octet
is always a symbol — so 128 values suffice. Every undecodable octet decodes with width 1, so *n* bad octets
always become *n* escapes. And U+DC80–U+DCFF are low surrogates: never Unicode scalar values, so well-formed
text can never produce one and an escape can never be mistaken for content. (The scheme is Python's
`surrogateescape`, PEP 383; Rust's WTF-8 answers the same problem the same way.)

**A string is its octets, so building one joins octets.** Every member and operator that builds a string — `+`,
`append`, `prepend`, `push`, `replace`, `pad_start`/`pad_end`, f-strings — concatenates the octets, and the result is
read afresh: escapes whose octets meet to complete a sequence read as the one symbol they spell.
[`runes`](runes.md) holds symbols, so the same building keeps them apart; the octets are the same either
way.

```go
a = bytes([0xE2, 0x82]).string()  // two escapes: the first two octets of "₩"
b = bytes([0xA9]).string()        // one escape: its last octet
(a + b).len()                     // => 1 — the octets meet and read "₩"
a + b == "₩"                      // => true
a.runes().append(b).len()         // => 3 — runes keeps the three escapes
```

**The two places this is visible elsewhere.** A [`rune`](rune.md)'s domain is exactly what can be encoded
— scalar values plus the 128 escapes — so `rune(0xDCFF)` exists while `rune(0xD800)` raises where it is written, and
no conversion *out* of `rune`/`runes` can fail. And the boundary **out** of the language is not total: `json.encode`
raises on text holding escapes, because JSON text is UTF-8 by definition. Encode the `bytes` instead (they go as
base64), or repair the text first.

## The blank set

The no-argument form of the match members acts on the type's **blank set** — its notion of insignificant
content. For `string` that is **NUL ∪ Unicode whitespace** (the Unicode `White_Space` class): this is what
no-arg `trim()`, `split()`, `partition()`, `index()`, `count()`, `keep()`, and `remove()` act on, and the
default `pad_start`/`pad_end` fill is the set's canonical member, the space.

Being the Unicode class, it includes the non-breaking space and every other Unicode space — not just ASCII
whitespace:

```go
"\u00a0x".trim()     // => "x" — the NBSP is blank
"\x00x\x00".trim()   // => "x" — NUL is blank
```

`bytes` projects the same notion into its element domain (the ASCII subset — all the whitespace an octet can
express); the sets agree wherever the domains overlap.

## Callbacks

A member that takes a function — the predicate reading of the match members, `map`, `flat_map`, `for_each`, `reduce`
— calls it in the **fewest form it accepts**, read from the callable's arity and whether it is variadic, never from
what kind of callable it is:

- a per-element callback gets the element when it accepts one argument, else `(index, element)`; anything else
raises;
- a `reduce` callback gets `(acc, element)` when it accepts two arguments, else `(acc, index, element)`; anything
else raises.

So `func(x, ...rest)` and `func(...args)` get the element, and a builtin or a bound member is a callback like any
other (`min` and `"abc".contains` accept one argument). A lambda is the one way to call a callable in another form —
choose the form, reorder, fix or drop arguments:

```go
"abc".count(func(i, c) { return i > 0 })               // => 2 — accepts two, not one
"abc".index(func(c, ...rest) { return c == 'b' })     // => 1 — accepts one: the element
"abcd".keep("bd".contains)                            // => "bd"
"abc".reduce("", (s, c) => c + s)                      // => "cba"
```

<a id="all"></a>
### `all(...x) -> bool`

Report whether every element matches a value, a set or a predicate; with no argument, whether every element is significant; see [`any`](#any).

A function argument gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument
([callbacks](#callbacks)).

<a id="any"></a>
### `any(...x) -> bool`

Report whether some element matches a value, a set or a predicate; with no argument, whether any element is significant.

A function argument gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument
([callbacks](#callbacks)).

`any`/`all` take a value, a function, or nothing — the contiguous-run query belongs to `contains`:

```go
"abc".all(func(c) { return c >= 'a' })    // => true
"abc".any("ab")              // Error: invalid_argument_type: "all/any of a run" has no reading — use contains
```

<a id="append"></a>
### `append(...xs) -> string`

Add the arguments at the back as whole operands: text spreads as a run, a symbol is one element.

`x.append(a, b)` ≡ `x + a + b`.

Whole operands in order, mixing runs and elements freely: `x.append("ab", 'c')` ≡ `x + "ab" + 'c'`.

```go
"x".append("ab", 'c', 98)    // => "xabcb" — 98 is 'b'
"ab".append(bytes("cd"))     // => "abcd"
"c".prepend("a", 'b')        // => "abc" — arguments in order, at the front
```

<a id="array"></a>
### `array([default]) -> array`

Re-represent the text as an array of its symbols, each a `rune`.

```go
"abé".array()        // => ['a', 'b', 'é'] — an array of runes
```

The `default` is taken for interface uniformity — every conversion carries it — and is never used: the
conversion is total.

<a id="bool"></a>
### `bool([default]) -> bool`

Parse the text as a `bool`: `true`/`false`, `1`/`0`, `t`/`f`, `yes`/`no`, case-insensitive.

```go
"Yes".bool()         // => true — true/false, 1/0, t/f, yes/no — case-insensitive
"maybe".bool()       // Error: conversion
```

<a id="bytes"></a>
### `bytes([default]) -> bytes`

Re-represent the text as its octets, the UTF-8 encoding.

```go
"héllo".bytes().len()  // => 6 — octets — the UTF-8 encoding
```

The `default` is taken for interface uniformity — every conversion carries it — and is never used: the
conversion is total.

<a id="camel_case"></a>
### `camel_case() -> string`

Render the text as a `camelCase` identifier; see [`snake_case`](#snake_case).

<a id="case_fold"></a>
### `case_fold() -> string`

Answer the canonical case fold, so that `a.case_fold() == b.case_fold()` is exact case-insensitive equality.

`case_fold()` is the canonical fold: each fold orbit maps to its smallest lowercase member (else the smallest
member), so `a.case_fold() == b.case_fold()` is exact case-insensitive equality. Because it is a transform —
not a comparison predicate — the result composes: it works as a dict key, a sort basis, a dedup basis.
`.lower()` comparison is not a substitute; they differ in both directions:

```go
"Hello".case_fold()                                   // => "hello"
"ſtraße".case_fold() == "Straße".case_fold()          // => true — long s ſ and S both fold to s
"İstanbul".case_fold() == "istanbul".case_fold()      // => false — İ keeps its own identity, distinct from i
```

<a id="chunk"></a>
### `chunk(n) -> array`

Split into strings of up to `n` symbols, answered as an array.

```go
"abcde".chunk(2)             // => ["ab", "cd", "e"]
```

<a id="contains"></a>
### `contains(...x) -> bool`

Report whether an element, a run, a member of a set or a predicate match occurs; with no argument, whether any element is significant.

A function argument gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument
([callbacks](#callbacks)).

It takes all five readings: element, run, variadic set, predicate, and no-argument (any element outside the blank
set).

No-argument `contains()` ≡ `any()` asks "any significant content?" — `"   ".contains()` is `false`. The
contiguous-run query belongs to `contains`: `any`/`all` take no run.

```go
"banana".contains("nan")     // => true
```

<a id="copy"></a>
### `copy() -> string`

Answer the receiver, which as an immutable string already is an independent copy.

On an immutable value `copy`/`freeze` are cheap identity-like operations kept for generic code.

<a id="count"></a>
### `count(...x) -> int`

Count the matches of an element, a run (non-overlapping occurrences), a set or a predicate; with no argument, the significant elements.

A function argument gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument
([callbacks](#callbacks)).

```go
"banana".count("na")         // => 2
```

<a id="date"></a>
### `date([default]) -> date`

Parse the text as a `date` in the strict `YYYY-MM-DD` form, as `date(text)` reads it; bad text raises unless a default is given.

Any other spelling names its layout: see [`parse_date`](#parse_date).

```go
"2026-08-29".date().day()   // => 29
```

<a id="decimal"></a>
### `decimal([default]) -> decimal`

Parse the text as a `decimal`; bad text raises unless a default is given.

<a id="dedup"></a>
### `dedup() -> string`

Collapse each run of equal neighbours to one element.

```go
"aabbaa".dedup()             // => "aba"
```

<a id="first"></a>
### `first([default]) -> rune`

Answer the first element; an empty string raises unless a default is given.

<a id="flat_map"></a>
### `flat_map(fn) -> string`

Map each element through the callback, then concatenate: a run result splices in, `undefined` is dropped.

The callback gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument ([callbacks](#callbacks)).

```go
"a-b".flat_map(func(c) { return c == '-' ? " / " : c })  // => "a / b"
"a-b".flat_map(func(c) { return c == '-' ? undefined : c })  // => "ab" — undefined dropped
```

<a id="float"></a>
### `float([default]) -> float`

Parse the text as a `float`; bad text raises unless a default is given.

```go
"1.5".float()        // => 1.5
```

<a id="for_each"></a>
### `for_each(fn) -> string`

Call the callback on every element — always a **full pass**, its return value ignored — and return the receiver.

The callback gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument ([callbacks](#callbacks)).

Early exit is `break`'s job in a `for` loop; returning the receiver lets it chain.

```go
io := import("io")
"abc".for_each(func(c) { io.print(c) })               // prints each symbol, returns "abc"
```

<a id="format"></a>
### `format([spec]) -> string`

Render the value per the [format mini-language](../../format_mini_language.md).

```go
"hi".format("q")     // => "\"hi\"" — quoted render
```

<a id="freeze"></a>
### `freeze() -> string`

Answer the receiver, which as a string already is deep-immutable; see [`copy`](#copy).

```go
is_immutable("abc")  // => true — free predicate — always, for string
```

<a id="has_prefix"></a>
### `has_prefix(x, ...more) -> bool`

Report whether the string starts with the element or run, or with any of a set of them.

No predicate reading ("the first symbol satisfies `f`" is `index(f) == 0`).

```go
"foobar".has_prefix('f')            // => true
"foobar".has_prefix("x", "fo")      // => true — run set
```

<a id="has_suffix"></a>
### `has_suffix(x, ...more) -> bool`

Report whether the string ends with the element or run, or with any of a set of them; see [`has_prefix`](#has_prefix).

<a id="index"></a>
### `index([x[, default]]) -> int`

Answer the first position of a match of an element, a run or a predicate, or `undefined` (the `default` when given) on a miss.

A function argument gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument
([callbacks](#callbacks)).

`index` and [`index_last`](#index_last) are the only locators.

A locator miss answers `undefined` — never `-1` — or the trailing default. The position is a symbol offset,
usable with `s[i]`.

```go
"banana".index("na")         // => 2
"banana".index_last("na")    // => 4
"banana".index("xy")         // => undefined — miss — never -1
"banana".index("xy", -1)     // => -1 — explicit default
"héllo".index('l')           // => 2 — symbol offset, usable with s[i]
"abc".index(func(c) { return c == 'b' })  // => 1
"  ab".index()               // => 2 — no argument: first significant symbol
```

<a id="index_last"></a>
### `index_last([x[, default]]) -> int`

Answer the last position of a match, or `undefined` (the `default` when given) on a miss; see [`index`](#index).

<a id="insert"></a>
### `insert(i, ...items) -> string`

Insert each argument as one element at position `i`.

An edit position out of `[0, len]` raises.

```go
"ad".insert(1, 'b', 'c')     // => "abcd"
"ab".insert(2, 'c')          // => "abc" — position len is valid
"ab".insert(3, 'c')          // Error: index_out_of_bounds: 3 out of range [0, 2]
```

<a id="int"></a>
### `int([default]) -> int`

Parse the text as an `int`; bad text raises unless a default is given.

```go
"123".int()          // => 123
"12a".int()          // Error: conversion: cannot convert string to int
"12a".int(0)         // => 0
```

<a id="is_ascii"></a>
### `is_ascii() -> bool`

Report whether every octet is below `0x80`, which also means one octet per symbol.

```go
"abc".is_ascii()                      // => true
"abé".is_ascii()                      // => false
```

<a id="is_empty"></a>
### `is_empty() -> bool`

Report whether the string has no elements.

<a id="is_true"></a>
### `is_true() -> bool`

Report truthiness, which is non-emptiness: `!!x` ⟺ `x != string()`.

<a id="is_valid"></a>
### `is_valid() -> bool`

Report whether every symbol is a real symbol, with no [octet escapes](#undecodable-octets).

The text is well-formed UTF-8 exactly when this holds.

```go
"abc".is_valid()                      // => true
bytes([97, 255]).string().is_valid()  // => false
```

<a id="kebab_case"></a>
### `kebab_case() -> string`

Render the text as a `kebab-case` identifier; see [`snake_case`](#snake_case).

<a id="keep"></a>
### `keep(...x) -> string`

Keep only the matches of an element, a run, a set or a predicate; with no argument, the significant elements; see [`remove`](#remove).

A function argument gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument
([callbacks](#callbacks)).

<a id="last"></a>
### `last([default]) -> rune`

Answer the last element; an empty string raises unless a default is given.

<a id="len"></a>
### `len() -> int`

Answer the number of elements — symbols, not octets.

<a id="lower"></a>
### `lower() -> string`

Map every symbol to lowercase.

```go
"héllo".upper()      // => "HÉLLO"
"HÉLLO".lower()      // => "héllo"
```

<a id="map"></a>
### `map(fn) -> string`

Answer a `string` of the callback's results, strictly 1:1: each result must be exactly one symbol.

The callback gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument ([callbacks](#callbacks)).

The callback must return exactly one symbol per element; a sequence or `undefined` result raises.

```go
"abc".map(func(c) { return (c.int() + 1).rune() })       // => "bcd"
"abc".map(func(c) { return "xx" })   // Error: invalid_value: map is 1:1 — the concatenating form is flat_map
```

<a id="max"></a>
### `max([default]) -> rune`

Answer the largest element; an empty string raises unless a default is given.

<a id="min"></a>
### `min([default]) -> rune`

Answer the smallest element; an empty string raises unless a default is given.

<a id="nanoseconds"></a>
### `nanoseconds([default]) -> int`

Parse the text as a duration in nanoseconds, in Go's duration grammar (`"300ms"`, `"-1.5h"`).

```go
"1h30m".nanoseconds()    // => 5400000000000 — a duration, in Go's duration grammar ("300ms", "-1.5h")
"later".nanoseconds(0)   // => 0
```

<a id="pad_end"></a>
### `pad_end(n[, fill]) -> string`

Pad at the back with the fill element until length `n`; see [`pad_start`](#pad_start).

<a id="pad_start"></a>
### `pad_start(n[, fill]) -> string`

Pad at the front with the fill element until length `n`.

Pad to symbol width `n` with one fill element (default: the space, the blank set's canonical member). A run fill
raises; a width at or below `len()` is a no-op, and one past `4294967296` symbols raises rather than exhausting
the host.

```go
"7".pad_start(3)                    // => "  7"
"7".pad_start(3, '0')               // => "007"
"7".pad_start(3, "ab")              // Error: invalid_argument_type: one fill element, not a run
```

<a id="parse_date"></a>
### `parse_date(layout[, default]) -> date`

Parse the text as a `date` under a layout; text the layout does not read raises unless a default is given.

`"date"` reads the strict `YYYY-MM-DD` form, any other layout is read as for [`parse_time`](#parse_time) (see
[date](date.md)); the default comes after the layout.

```go
"29/08/2026".parse_date("%d/%m/%Y").month()   // => 8
```

<a id="parse_time"></a>
### `parse_time(layout[, default]) -> time`

Parse the text as a `time` under a [layout](time.md#text-layouts); text the layout does not read raises unless a default is given.

A malformed layout always raises (`invalid_value`): it is the script's mistake, not the data's. The default
comes after the layout.

```go
"2026-08-29T00:00:00Z".parse_time("iso").year()   // => 2026 — the canonical grammar
"29/08/2026".parse_time("%d/%m/%Y").day()          // => 29
"nope".parse_time("iso", time())                   // => time("1970-01-01T00:00:00Z") — the default, after the layout
```

<a id="partition"></a>
### `partition(...seps) -> array`

Split at the first separator hit into exactly three pieces, `[before, sep, after]`.

`partition` answers exactly three pieces, `[before, sep, after]`, splitting at the first hit; a miss answers
`[s, "", ""]`. With no argument the separator is the whole first maximal run of blank filler. Separators take
the same menu as [`split`](#split).

```go
"key=value=x".partition('=')     // => ["key", "=", "value=x"]
"abc".partition('=')             // => ["abc", "", ""]
"key  value rest".partition()    // => ["key", "  ", "value rest"]
```

<a id="pascal_case"></a>
### `pascal_case() -> string`

Render the text as a `PascalCase` identifier; see [`snake_case`](#snake_case).

<a id="prepend"></a>
### `prepend(...xs) -> string`

Add the arguments at the front as whole operands, in argument order; see [`append`](#append).

<a id="push"></a>
### `push(...items) -> string`

Add each argument at the back as exactly **one element**; a sequence argument raises, even at length 1.

**Validating**: the refusal is the member's purpose — use it when appending a run would be a bug.

```go
"ab".push('c')               // => "abc"
"ab".push("c")               // Error: invalid_argument_type: push takes one element, never a sequence
```

<a id="push_first"></a>
### `push_first(...items) -> string`

Add each argument at the front as exactly one element, in argument order; see [`push`](#push).

<a id="reduce"></a>
### `reduce(init, fn) -> value`

Fold the elements left to right into an accumulator that starts at `init`.

The callback gets `(acc, element)`, or `(acc, index, element)` when it does not accept two arguments
([callbacks](#callbacks)).

```go
"abc".reduce(0, func(acc, c) { return acc + c.int() })   // => 294
```

<a id="remove"></a>
### `remove(...x) -> string`

Remove every match of an element, a run, a set or a predicate; with no argument, the elements of the [blank set](#the-blank-set).

A function argument gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument
([callbacks](#callbacks)).

`remove` and [`keep`](#keep) are duals over the same readings, and the names say which way each one goes.

`keep(x)` answers the matching symbols, `remove(x)` answers the rest — the direction is in the name; both take
the full menu and act on every occurrence. With no argument each reads against the blank set the way its own
verb implies — `keep()` keeps the significant symbols, `remove()` removes the blank ones — so the two land on
the same answer by two different routes:

```go
"a1b2".keep(func(c) { return c >= '0' && c <= '9' })   // => "12"
"banana".remove("na")        // => "ba"
" a b ".keep()             // => "ab"
" a b ".remove()             // => "ab" — removes the blanks — same answer, the other action
```

<a id="remove_prefix"></a>
### `remove_prefix(x, ...more) -> string`

Remove the element or run — or the longest of a set of them — once, anchored at the front; absent → unchanged.

Given several, the longest that matches is removed; a miss answers the receiver unchanged.

```go
"foobar".remove_prefix("foo")       // => "bar"
"foobar".remove_prefix("bar")       // => "foobar" — miss: unchanged
"file.txt".remove_suffix(".txt", ".md")  // => "file"
```

<a id="remove_suffix"></a>
### `remove_suffix(x, ...more) -> string`

Remove the element or run — or the longest of a set of them — once, anchored at the back; absent → unchanged; see [`remove_prefix`](#remove_prefix).

<a id="repeat"></a>
### `repeat(n) -> string`

Concatenate the string with itself `n` times; `s * n` is the operator form.

`n` must be a non-negative whole number (`2.0` converts, `1.5` raises). `s * n` is the operator form — same
count slot, same errors. There is no reflected `n * s`, and a result past `4294967296` symbols raises rather
than exhausting the host.

```go
"ab".repeat(3)               // => "ababab"
"ab" * 3                     // => "ababab" — the operator form
"-" * 40                     // => "----------------------------------------"
3 * "ab"                     // Error: invalid_binary_operator: int * string — no reflected direction
"ab".repeat(1.5)             // Error: invalid_value: whole number required — never silent truncation
```

<a id="replace"></a>
### `replace(old, new) -> string`

Replace every occurrence of `old`, an element or a run, with `new`.

Element or run in both positions; never variadic, never a predicate.

```go
"banana".replace("na", "NO")        // => "baNONO"
"banana".replace('a', "oo")         // => "boonoonoo" — element out, run in
```

<a id="reverse"></a>
### `reverse() -> string`

Reverse the order of the elements.

```go
"abc".reverse()              // => "cba"
```

<a id="runes"></a>
### `runes([default]) -> runes`

Re-represent the text as `runes`, the O(1)-indexing form.

```go
"abc".runes()        // => u"abc" — the O(1)-indexing form
```

The `default` is taken for interface uniformity — every conversion carries it — and is never used: the
conversion is total.

<a id="slice"></a>
### `slice([start[, end]]) -> string`

Answer the symbols from `start` to `end`; bounds **clamp** (contrast `splice`, which raises), negative indices count from the end.

`slice` **clamps** out-of-range bounds (reading past the end is harmless); negative indices count from the
end. Equivalent to `s[start:end]` with a name usable in a chain; offsets are symbols.

```go
"hello".slice(1, 3)          // => "el"
"hello".slice(3, 99)         // => "lo" — clamps
"hello".slice(-3, -1)        // => "ll"
```

<a id="snake_case"></a>
### `snake_case() -> string`

Render the text as a `snake_case` identifier.

The four **identifier renderings** segment the text fully and normalise each word's interior. Word boundaries
are: runs of whitespace/`_`/`-` (discarded); a lower→upper transition; and in an upper run followed by a
lower, the last upper starts the new word (`parseXMLFile` → `parse` | `XML` | `File`). The boundary set is
closed — digits, apostrophes, and periods stay inside words:

```go
"parseXMLFile".snake_case()      // => "parse_xml_file"
"Parse XML file".kebab_case()    // => "parse-xml-file"
"parse_xml_file".camel_case()    // => "parseXmlFile" — interior normalised
"parse xml file".pascal_case()   // => "ParseXmlFile"
"don't stop".snake_case()        // => "don't_stop" — the apostrophe is not a boundary
```

<a id="sort"></a>
### `sort() -> string`

Order the symbols by code point; there is no comparator.

```go
"banana".sort()              // => "aaabnn"
```

<a id="splice"></a>
### `splice([start[, delete_count]]) -> string` / `splice(start, delete_count, ...items) -> string`

Removes `delete_count` elements at `start`, then inserts the items there.

`splice` **raises** out of range (editing past the end is not harmless). Its inserts take the add-side
reading: runs spread, scalars are one element, anything else raises.

```go
"abcd".splice(1, 2, "XY", 'z')  // => "aXYzd"
"ad".splice(1, 0, 'b')       // => "abd"
"ab".splice(5, 1)            // Error: index_out_of_bounds: 5 out of range [0, 2]
```

<a id="split"></a>
### `split(...seps) -> array`

Split the text into an array of the pieces between the separators.

Separators take the menu: element, run, homogeneous set, element-level predicate, or absent (the blank set).
**`split` has no limit argument.**

Two regimes, deliberately different:

- An **explicit separator** keeps empty pieces — n hits make n+1 pieces, so `"".split(",")` is `[""]`.
- The **no-argument form** yields the maximal runs of significant content — empties never appear, and
splitting pure filler yields `[]`.
- An empty-run separator matches nothing: `"ab".split("")` is `["ab"]`.

```go
"a,b,,c".split(',')          // => ["a", "b", "", "c"] — empties kept
"a::b::c".split("::")        // => ["a", "b", "c"]
"a,b;c".split(',', ';')      // => ["a", "b", "c"] — separator set
"a1b2c".split(func(c) { return c >= '0' && c <= '9' })  // => ["a", "b", "c"]
"  a  b\tc ".split()         // => ["a", "b", "c"] — blank set, maximal runs
"   ".split()                // => []
"".split(",")                // => [""]
```

<a id="split_lines"></a>
### `split_lines() -> array`

Split the text into an array of its lines at `\n`, `\r\n` or `\r`; a trailing line break adds no empty last line.

```go
"a\nb\r\nc\n".split_lines()  // => ["a", "b", "c"]
```

<a id="string"></a>
### `string([default]) -> string`

Answer the receiver: a string is immutable and identity-less, so there is nothing to construct.

The mutable-bodied types copy instead: see [`array()`](array.md#array).

<a id="time"></a>
### `time([default]) -> time`

Parse the text as a `time` in the canonical grammar, as `time(text)` reads it; bad text raises unless a default is given.

Any other spelling names its layout: see [`parse_time`](#parse_time).

```go
"2026-08-29T00:00:00Z".time().year()   // => 2026
"nope".time(time())                    // => time("1970-01-01T00:00:00Z") — the default
```

<a id="title_case"></a>
### `title_case() -> string`

Render the text as a label: each word's first symbol uppercased, the interior preserved.

`title_case()` is the **label rendering**: it segments on written boundaries only (whitespace/`_`/`-`),
uppercases each word's first symbol, and **preserves** the interior — a label keeps the author's emphasis:

```go
"ATM fee".title_case()           // => "ATM Fee"
"iPhone".title_case()            // => "IPhone"
"hELLO world".title_case()       // => "HELLO World"
"atm_fee-total".title_case()     // => "Atm Fee Total"
```

<a id="trim"></a>
### `trim(...set) -> string`

Repeatedly drop the elements at both ends while they belong to the set (the blank set with no argument).

Strip **a set of elements**, repeating while they match. A run argument raises — the anchored-run form is
`remove_prefix`/`remove_suffix`. No argument trims the [blank set](#the-blank-set).

```go
"  hi  ".trim()                     // => "hi"
"xxhixy".trim('x', 'y')             // => "hi"
"abhiab".trim("ab")                 // Error: invalid_argument_type: trim takes elements — spell trim('a', 'b')
```

<a id="trim_end"></a>
### `trim_end(...set) -> string`

Drop the trailing elements that belong to the set (the blank set with no argument); see [`trim`](#trim).

<a id="trim_start"></a>
### `trim_start(...set) -> string`

Drop the leading elements that belong to the set (the blank set with no argument); see [`trim`](#trim).

<a id="unique"></a>
### `unique() -> string`

Drop repeats, keeping each element at its first occurrence.

```go
"aabbaa".unique()            // => "ab"
```

<a id="upper"></a>
### `upper() -> string`

Map every symbol to uppercase; see [`lower`](#lower).
